faq.q: Can I give customers a discount for leaving a Google review?
faq.a: No. Google says offering free or discounted goods or services in exchange for reviews is fake engagement and is strictly prohibited. Reviews collected this way can be removed, and repeated violations can put your Business Profile at risk. You can ask every customer for an honest review, just don't reward them for it.

faq.q: How do I get my Google review link and QR code?
faq.a: On a computer, open your Business Profile at business.google.com, select Read reviews, then Get more reviews. Copy the link, and right-click the QR code to save it. Google currently generates review QR codes only in a computer browser, not on mobile.

faq.q: Is it okay to ask for Google reviews on WhatsApp?
faq.a: Yes. Google itself suggests sharing your review link by email, WhatsApp or social media. Send it to every customer, not only the happy ones, keep it to one message and one reminder, and never attach a discount or gift to the request.

faq.q: Why are my Google reviews disappearing?
faq.a: Google removes reviews it believes break its policies, for example reviews that were incentivised, posted from related or multiple accounts, or written with a conflict of interest such as by staff or family. Reviews can also vanish if the reviewer deletes them or their account. Asking all customers honestly, with no rewards, is the best protection.

faq.q: How do I remove a fake or negative Google review?
faq.a: You can't remove a genuine negative review, but you can report reviews that break Google's policies. Open the review in your Business Profile, select the three dots and choose Report review, then track it in Google's review management tool. Meanwhile, post a calm public reply so new customers see your side.

faq.q: Do replies to Google reviews help my ranking?
faq.a: Google lists responding to reviews among its tips to improve local ranking, and it says more reviews and positive ratings can help your business's local ranking. Replies also show new customers that a real person runs the business, which helps turn profile views into visits.

faq.q: How many Google reviews does a small business need?
faq.a: There's no magic number. Look at the top three businesses in your category on Google Maps near you and aim to match their count and rating, with a steady flow of recent reviews. Five to ten genuine reviews a week makes a visible difference within a few months.

faq.q: When is Diwali in 2026?
faq.a: Lakshmi Puja, the main Diwali day, is on Sunday, 8 November 2026. Dhanteras is on Friday, 6 November, Govardhan Puja on Tuesday, 10 November, and Bhai Dooj on Wednesday, 11 November. Puja muhurat times vary by city.

faq.q: Is it too late to start Diwali marketing on Google?
faq.a: No. Most Google Business Profile changes, such as photos, offer posts and special hours, can be done in an afternoon. Posts and edits sometimes stay pending while Google reviews them, so make your changes at least a week before Dhanteras.

faq.q: Can I add Diwali Sale to my business name on Google?

faq.q: Why is my business not showing on Google Maps?
faq.a: The most common reasons are an unverified Business Profile, a suspended profile, a business name or address that breaks Google's guidelines, a wrong map pin, or simply a new profile that Google hasn't ranked yet. Start by checking verification and any notices in the Google Account that manages your profile.

faq.q: How long does it take for a new business to show on Google Maps?

faq.q: Why does my business show for its name but not for searches like near me?
faq.a: That's a ranking problem, not a visibility problem. Google ranks local results on relevance, distance and prominence. Choose the most specific primary category, complete every part of your profile, add recent photos and earn more reviews to improve relevance and prominence.

content.text: A customer stands outside your shop, types what you sell into Google Maps, and three other shops come up. Not yours. It happens to good, busy businesses every day in Mumbai, and the cause is almost never "Google doesn't like you". It's usually one of a handful of fixable problems: an unverified profile, a wrong category, a name that breaks the rules, or a profile Google can't trust.
This guide walks through every reason your business isn't showing on Google Maps or Search, in the order I check them during an audit, with the fix for each. Most take less than ten minutes.
The short version:

check that your profile is verified and not suspended, search while signed in to the right account, give new edits up to 3 days and new profiles up to a month, then fix your category, name, address and pin. If you show up but rank low, work on reviews, photos and complete information.
First, are you missing or just ranking low?
These are two different problems with different fixes. Search your exact business name plus your area on Google Maps (for example, "Sharma Sarees Andheri East").
You don't appear even for your own name:
it's a visibility problem. Start with fixes 1 to 6 below.
You appear for your name, but not for "saree shop near me":
it's a ranking problem. Jump to fixes 7 to 11.

content.text: Visibility problems: you don't show up at all
1. Your profile isn't verified
This is the big one. Google says plainly that
only verified businesses can show their business info on Maps and Search
. Open
business.google.com
while signed in. If you see a "Get verified" prompt, finish it. Google may ask for a short video of your shop, signage and tools of the trade, so film in daylight with your board clearly visible.
2. Your profile is suspended or disabled

If a profile breaks Google's guidelines, Google can disable or suspend it, and it stops showing to customers until the issue is fixed. Google sends a notice to the Google Account that manages the profile, so check that inbox (and its spam folder). Fix the cause first, usually the name, address or category, then request a review from inside your profile.
3. You're searching from the wrong account (or it's just new)

To see and manage your own profile, you need to be signed in to the Google Account linked to it. Search "my business" on Google, or open the Maps app and tap Business. Also give Google time: edits can take up to 3 days to appear, and Google says a new business can take up to a month to show in search rankings.
4. Your business name breaks the rules
Names like "Sharma Sarees – Best Saree Shop in Andheri" feel clever, but Google's
guidelines

say your name must match your real-world name, with no taglines, extra keywords or location details unless they're part of your actual name. Breaking this can get the profile suspended. Use the exact name on your signboard.
5. Your address or map pin is wrong

A typo in the address, the wrong building, or a pin dropped across the road makes Google less sure where you are. In my audits this is one of the most common problems: a misspelled street, a missing shop number, or a pin on the wrong side of a flyover. Check the full address word by word, then zoom in on the map and drag the pin onto your exact entrance.
6. There are duplicate listings of your business

Old listings created by staff, previous owners or customers split your reviews and confuse Google. Search your name and phone number on Maps. If you find a duplicate, use "Suggest an edit", then "Close or remove", then "Duplicate", or claim it and ask Google to merge it.
Ranking problems: you show up, but not where customers look
Google ranks local results on three things:
relevance
(how well your profile matches the search),
distance
(how far you are from the person searching) and
prominence
(how well known you are, including reviews and links). That's from
Google's own explanation
, which adds that there's no way to pay for a better local ranking. You can't change distance, so work on the other two.

content.text: 7. Your primary category is too broad or wrong

Your primary category decides which searches you're eligible for. A saree shop listed only as "Clothing store" competes with every clothes shop in the area. Pick the most specific category that describes your main business, then add up to a few secondary ones for the rest.
8. Your profile is incomplete

Fill in everything Google offers: hours, phone, website, services or products with prices, attributes like wheelchair access or online payments, and a description in plain language. Google lists complete, accurate information as the first way to improve your local ranking.
9. You have few reviews, or a low rating

Google says more reviews and positive ratings can help your local ranking, and replying to reviews shows you value feedback. If your competitors have 300 reviews and you have 12, that gap is hurting you. My guide on
how to get more Google reviews
has a 30-day plan with ready WhatsApp messages.
10. Your photos are old, few or missing

Profiles with real, recent photos look open and trustworthy. Add your shop front (so people recognise it from the street), the inside, your products, and your team. Google recommends adding photos and videos to show customers what you offer.
11. Your website doesn't back up your profile

Prominence also comes from what the rest of the web says about you. A simple website with your exact name, address and phone number, a page for each main service, and links from local directories helps Google trust your profile. If you don't have one, a
small business website
is one of the best long-term investments for local search.
Address problems that are common in Indian cities
Indian addresses are messy, and Google's systems have to match yours against what customers, delivery apps and other maps say. These are the patterns I see most often in Mumbai audits:
Missing shop or unit number.
In a building or market with 40 shops, "Sunrise Shopping Centre, Andheri East" isn't enough. Add your shop number and floor.
Different spellings of the same place.
"Gundavali", "Gundawali" and "Gundvali" may all appear online. Use the spelling on your signboard and official documents, and use it the same way everywhere.
A name in two languages.

If your board shows the name in Marathi or Hindi as well as English, use the English name in your profile and keep it identical across Google, your website and directories, rather than creating a second listing in the other language.
Landmarks inside the address.
"Opp. station" and "Near Vishal Hall" help people, but they belong in your description or directions, not in the business name.
Home-based and service businesses.

If customers don't visit you, such as a home tutor, an electrician or a caterer, set a service area and hide your home address, rather than using a fake shop address. Google's guidelines don't allow virtual offices or addresses you don't actually operate from.
What not to do when your profile is suspended
Don't create a new profile.
It's tempting, but duplicate profiles for the same business break Google's guidelines and usually make things worse.
Don't keep editing randomly.
Every edit can trigger another review. Fix the specific problem (usually the name, address or category) once, then request reinstatement.
Don't pay anyone who promises "instant reinstatement".
Only Google can reinstate a profile. Keep proof ready instead: shop photos with your signboard, a utility bill or GST certificate in the business name, and a short video of the premises.

Hidden until the issue is fixed and the profile is reinstated

If a profile breaks Google's guidelines, Google can disable or suspend it, and it stops showing to customers until the issue is fixed. Google sends a notice to the Google Account that manages the profile, so check that inbox (and its spam folder). Fix the cause first, usually the name, address or category, then request a review from inside your profile.

3. You're searching from the wrong account (or it's just new)

To see and manage your own profile, you need to be signed in to the Google Account linked to it. Search "my business" on Google, or open the Maps app and tap Business. Also give Google time: edits can take up to 3 days to appear, and Google says a new business can take up to a month to show in search rankings.

4. Your business name breaks the rules

Names like "Sharma Sarees – Best Saree Shop in Andheri" feel clever, but Google's guidelines say your name must match your real-world name, with no taglines, extra keywords or location details unless they're part of your actual name. Breaking this can get the profile suspended. Use the exact name on your signboard.

5. Your address or map pin is wrong

A typo in the address, the wrong building, or a pin dropped across the road makes Google less sure where you are. Check the full address word by word, then zoom in on the map and drag the pin onto your exact entrance.

6. There are duplicate listings of your business

Old listings created by staff, previous owners or customers split your reviews and confuse Google. Search your name and phone number on Maps. If you find a duplicate, use "Suggest an edit", then "Close or remove", then "Duplicate", or claim it and ask Google to merge it.

Ranking problems: you show up, but not where customers look

Google ranks local results on three things: relevance (how well your profile matches the search), distance (how far you are from the person searching) and prominence (how well known you are, including reviews and links). That's from Google's own explanation, which adds that there's no way to pay for a better local ranking. You can't change distance, so work on the other two.

7. Your primary category is too broad or wrong

Your primary category decides which searches you're eligible for. A saree shop listed only as "Clothing store" competes with every clothes shop in the area. Pick the most specific category that describes your main business, then add up to a few secondary ones for the rest.

8. Your profile is incomplete

Fill in everything Google offers: hours, phone, website, services or products with prices, attributes like wheelchair access or online payments, and a description in plain language. Google lists complete, accurate information as the first way to improve your local ranking.

9. You have few reviews, or a low rating

Google says more reviews and positive ratings can help your local ranking, and replying to reviews shows you value feedback. If your competitors have 300 reviews and you have 12, that gap is hurting you. My guide on how to get more Google reviews has a 30-day plan with ready WhatsApp messages.

10. Your photos are old, few or missing

Profiles with real, recent photos look open and trustworthy. Add your shop front (so people recognise it from the street), the inside, your products, and your team. Google recommends adding photos and videos to show customers what you offer.

11. Your website doesn't back up your profile

Prominence also comes from what the rest of the web says about you. A simple website with your exact name, address and phone number, a page for each main service, and links from local directories helps Google trust your profile. If you don't have one, a small business website is one of the best long-term investments for local search.

Address problems that are common in Indian cities

Indian addresses are messy, and Google's systems have to match yours against what customers, delivery apps and other maps say. These are the patterns I see most often in Mumbai audits:

  • Missing shop or unit number. In a building or market with 40 shops, "Sunrise Shopping Centre, Andheri East" isn't enough. Add your shop number and floor.

  • Different spellings of the same place. "Gundavali", "Gundawali" and "Gundvali" may all appear online. Use the spelling on your signboard and official documents, and use it the same way everywhere.

  • A name in two languages. If your board shows the name in Marathi or Hindi as well as English, use the English name in your profile and keep it identical across Google, your website and directories, rather than creating a second listing in the other language.

  • Landmarks inside the address. "Opp. station" and "Near Vishal Hall" help people, but they belong in your description or directions, not in the business name.

  • Home-based and service businesses. If customers don't visit you, such as a home tutor, an electrician or a caterer, set a service area and hide your home address, rather than using a fake shop address. Google's guidelines don't allow virtual offices or addresses you don't actually operate from.

What not to do when your profile is suspended

  • Don't create a new profile. It's tempting, but duplicate profiles for the same business break Google's guidelines and usually make things worse.

  • Don't keep editing randomly. Every edit can trigger another review. Fix the specific problem (usually the name, address or category) once, then request reinstatement.

  • Don't pay anyone who promises "instant reinstatement". Only Google can reinstate a profile. Keep proof ready instead: shop photos with your signboard, a utility bill or GST certificate in the business name, and a short video of the premises.

faq.q: Do Instagram posts show up on Google?

faq.q: How do I stop my Instagram posts showing on Google?
faq.a: Turn off the search engine option in your Instagram privacy settings, make your account private, or switch from a professional account to a personal one. Content that's already indexed can take time to disappear from search engines.

For a local shop, this is a free second chance at every search. This guide explains what changed, how to check your account is eligible, and how to write captions and reels that Google can understand, without turning your Instagram into a keyword dump.

The short version: use a public business or creator account, write captions that say what the product is, where you are and the price, use alt text and on-screen text, put your area and category in your bio, and link Instagram and your Google Business Profile to each other.

What changed, exactly

  • Who's included: public, professional (business or creator) accounts of people over 18.

  • What's included: photos, videos and reels posted from 1 January 2020 onwards.

  • How to opt out: turn the option off in your privacy settings, switch to a private account, or switch back to a personal account.

Why it matters: in Google's 2025 India study of festive shoppers, nearly 7 in 10 Facebook and Instagram users went to Google Search after seeing a brand (Think with Google, 2026). Your customers already move between the two. Now your Instagram content can meet them on Google too.

Step 1: Check your account is eligible

  1. Make sure your account is public.

  2. Switch to a professional account (business or creator) in Settings, under the account type and tools section, if you haven't already.

  3. Look in your privacy settings for the option that lets public photos and videos appear in search engine results, and make sure it's on.

Step 2: Write captions that Google can read

Search engines can't watch your reel the way a person does. They rely heavily on the text around it. A caption like "Festive vibes ✨🔥" tells Google nothing. Compare:

Weak caption

Search-friendly caption

Festive vibes ✨🔥

New Banarasi silk sarees for Diwali, from ₹4,500. In store now at our Andheri East shop, open till 10 pm.

New stock alert!!

Fresh 18 mm marine plywood and laminates in 40 shades. Free delivery across Andheri and Jogeshwari.

Weekend mood 💇‍♀️

Keratin treatment for frizzy hair at our Lokhandwala salon. Book a slot on WhatsApp.

The pattern: what it is + who it's for + where you are + price or offer + how to buy. Put the most important words in the first line, because that's what shows in search results. Keep emojis and hashtags, just don't let them replace the words.

Step 3: Make reels and photos readable

  • Add alt text to photo posts (Advanced settings, then Accessibility) describing the product: "Red Banarasi silk saree with gold zari border".

  • Put a short text line on the reel's opening frame, such as "Diwali saree collection 2026", and say the key words out loud. Instagram generates captions from speech, and those words help people and search engines understand the video.

  • Name the place. Add your shop as the location tag on every post.

Step 4: Turn your profile into a mini landing page

Your username, name field and bio are the most visible text on your profile. Use your real business name, your main category and your area: "Sharma Sarees | Silk & Bridal Sarees, Andheri East". Add your phone or WhatsApp, timings and a link to your website or Google profile. Highlights for "Prices", "Location" and "Reviews" answer the questions buyers have before they visit.

Step 5: Connect Instagram and Google both ways

Add your Instagram profile link to your Google Business Profile, and link your Google profile or website from your Instagram bio. Then reuse your best photos and reels on your Google profile. Google lets you add photos and videos to show what you offer, and fresh visual content tells shoppers you're active. When someone finds you on one platform, the other should confirm the same name, address, prices and photos.

Post on Instagram first, then upload the same photo or video to your Google Business Profile the same day. It takes two minutes and keeps both profiles fresh.

Step 6: Measure what's working

In Instagram Insights, check how many people reached your posts from outside your followers. In your Google Business Profile, watch calls, direction requests and website clicks. If a type of post (say, price-led reels) brings more profile visits and calls, make more of it. If you have a website with Google Analytics, you'll also see visits arriving from your Instagram link.

A 20-second reel script you can reuse

  1. 0–3 seconds: on-screen text with the product and area: "Banarasi silk sarees, Andheri East".

  2. 3–12 seconds: show three pieces up close and say the price range out loud.

  3. 12–17 seconds: the shop front and board, so people recognise you when they arrive.

  4. 17–20 seconds: "WhatsApp us to reserve, open till 10 pm".

Saying the product, area and price out loud matters: the words in your reel's audio, captions and text are what help it get understood and found.

What to avoid

  • Hashtag stuffing. Thirty hashtags and no words help nobody. Five relevant hashtags plus a clear caption work better.

  • Different names everywhere. If Instagram says "Sharma Saree House" and Google says "Sharma Sarees", customers, and search engines, wonder whether it's the same shop.

  • Going private to "look exclusive". Private accounts can't be indexed by search engines at all.
